   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?

   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Caterpillar is a century-old leader in a mature, cyclical industry rather than a Rule Breaker in an emerging one. It does show some Rule Breaker traits, including a top brand, strong price momentum (up about 48% over 52 weeks) and frequent 'overvalued' commentary, but its CEO is a professional manager and its growth is moderate outside the data-center power boom.
summaries.buffett: Caterpillar has a durable brand-and-dealer moat, understandable economics and strong cash generation ($9.5B of MP&E free cash flow in 2025), which fit Buffett's quality tests. However, earnings are cyclical (there was a loss in 2016), and at about 33 times trailing earnings there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value Caterpillar's simple, durable franchise: a dominant brand, an exclusive dealer network and a large installed base feeding services. Inverting, the main ways to lose are cyclical downturns, Chinese low-cost competition and paying too much, and today's valuation (about 27 times forward earnings) argues for patience.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Caterpillar as a cyclical whose earnings swing with construction, mining and energy cycles, and he warned that cyclicals look cheapest at peak earnings. Its P/E of about 33 is well above its long-run growth target of 5-7% a year, and insiders are not buying, although the share count keeps falling through buybacks.
summaries.fisher: Caterpillar scores well on several Fisher points: sales capability through its dealer network, about $2.1B a year of R&D producing autonomy and new power products, and long-tenured management. Its markets are cyclical rather than steadily growing, and profit margins fell in 2025 before recovering in 2026.
summaries.graham: Caterpillar meets Graham's size, financial-strength and dividend-record tests and has grown EPS strongly over ten years (from a $0.11 loss in 2016 to $18.81 in 2025). It fails on his price criteria, with a P/E near 33 and P/B near 18, and its 2016 loss breaks the ten-year earnings record, so a defensive Graham investor would not buy at today's price.
summaries.thiel: Caterpillar is not a Zero-to-One business: its technology is better than rivals' but not ten times better, and it competes in an established market with Komatsu and Chinese makers. It does have durable distribution, a strong brand and timely exposure to data-center power demand.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for large secular trends bought at sensible prices with disciplined management. Caterpillar is a real beneficiary of AI data-center power demand and runs with cost discipline, but its core is cyclical heavy machinery and its valuation (P/FCF about 38) already prices in much of the power story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (Q2 2026 adjusted EPS up 73% with a $72B record backlog) and estimates are rising, which fits Druckenmiller's focus on improving fundamentals 18-24 months ahead. Against that, high interest rates weigh on construction, and the stock has already fallen about 30% from its peak, signalling that the market doubts how long the boom will last.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith seeks high returns on capital without leverage and resilient growth. Caterpillar's ROIC of about 18% and strong cash generation are decent, but its cyclicality, a gross margin of about 34% and a valuation near 38 times free cash flow make it a weak fit with 'buy good companies, don't overpay'.
summaries.greenblatt: Return on capital is good (ROIC about 18%), but the earnings yield is low, with EV/EBIT about 27, which is an earnings yield near 3.6%. Caterpillar would therefore rank poorly on the Magic Formula today.
summaries.akre: Caterpillar fits Akre's stool on business quality (a dominant brand, a dealer moat and high returns) and has capable, owner-minded management. The reinvestment leg is weaker, because most cash goes to buybacks and dividends rather than high-return internal growth, and the price is high.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach wants low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts. Caterpillar is low-risk and well understood, but nothing about it is distressed or mispriced at about 27 times forward earnings, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup is absent.
summaries.wood: Caterpillar is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense. It has some exposure to robotics (autonomous mining haulage) and energy (power generation for data centers), but it is an incumbent industrial with modest growth and no Wright's-law cost declines.
summaries.ackman: Caterpillar has many traits Ackman likes: a simple, predictable-over-a-cycle, free-cash-flow-generative business with a dominant position and high barriers to entry. Its cyclicality, consolidated leverage from Cat Financial and today's premium valuation make it a weaker fit for his 'at a discount to intrinsic value' rule.
summaries.sleep: Caterpillar does not follow Nomad's 'scale economics shared' model of passing savings to customers. Its moat comes from brand, dealers and installed-base services, and it is run for margin through the cycle rather than ever-lower prices.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, fast-growing markets with technology at the right moment. Caterpillar addresses large but mature markets, with a timely, growing niche in data-center power and autonomy, so it fits only partly.
summaries.nash: Caterpillar passes Nash's quality tests on brand, scale, earnings beats (four straight) and secular exposure to AI power. It fails several hard rules: consolidated debt of $45.1B exceeds cash of $6.7B, operating margin was below 20% in 2025, and the valuation (PEG about 1.45, DCF value well below the price) is unattractive.

momentum.evidence: The shares rose about 48% over the last 52 weeks and more than 50% year to date by early October 2026, nearly three times the S&P 500's gain, though they have since fallen about 30% from their peak.

g4.evidence: Caterpillar is led by experienced insiders (CEO Joe Creed, at the company since 1997) and owned about 73% by institutions such as Vanguard and BlackRock, but it has no famous activist or star backer.

g6.evidence: Commentators such as XTB (October 2026) say the price has run ahead of fundamentals at a forward P/E near 27-32, far above its historical range.

simple.evidence: It makes and services construction and mining machines, engines and turbines and finances them, which is easy to understand, though the cycle is hard to forecast.

b2.evidence: Results are cyclical: sales fell to $41.7B in 2020 and there was a loss in 2016, but the company has been profitable every year since and set records in 2023-2024.

integrity.evidence: Management sets transparent 2030 targets (5-7% sales CAGR, $6B-$15B MP&E free cash flow), returns most free cash flow ($7.9B in 2025) and has no governance controversies.

b6.evidence: Since the 2011 Bucyrus deal it has avoided large acquisitions, focusing on services, autonomy and organic capacity for power generation instead of empire-building.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 18%, but its 57% ROE is inflated by buybacks and consolidated debt, mostly Cat Financial's $34.5B of customer financing.

fcf.evidence: MP&E free cash flow was $9.5B in 2025, more than reported profit of $8.9B, and a record $5.1B in Q2 2026 alone.

b10.evidence: Profit per share rose from $5.46 in 2020 to $18.81 in 2025 while diluted shares fell from 548.6M to 472.3M, and market value is now about $344B.

safety.evidence: At about $749, trailing P/E of about 33 and P/FCF of about 38 put the stock well above a conservative value for a cyclical business.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 27 and a PEG of about 1.45 look rich against the company's own 5-7% long-run sales growth target.

mu5.evidence: Failure is unlikely given its brand, dealers and installed base, but a deep downturn in construction, mining or data-center spending would sharply cut profits.

reinvest.evidence: It is adding engine and turbine capacity (65 GW target by 2030) and building out services, but most cash goes to buybacks and dividends rather than high-return reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical, with an added data-center power growth story.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 33 is far above its 5-7% long-run sales growth target, even though 2026 EPS growth is about 40%.

runway.evidence: Services ($24B in 2025, $30B target), data-center power and autonomy offer growth, but core markets are mature.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count (diluted shares 548.6M in 2020 to 462.5M in Q2 2026), but insiders are not making open-market purchases.

ly8.evidence: It is a widely followed Dow component covered by about 28 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It is launching new machines, autonomy, larger gensets and turbines and is restarting a 10-MW gas engine platform to meet power demand.

fi3.evidence: About $2.1B a year of R&D has delivered industry-leading autonomous haulage and high-horsepower power products that are now winning data-center orders.

fi4.evidence: Its 150 independent dealers across 190 countries are the industry's strongest sales and service force.

longterm.evidence: Management invests through the cycle in capacity, technology and services under a plan to 'extend leadership into the next 100 years', while also keeping tight margin targets.

gr1.evidence: It had $67.6B of 2025 sales and a market value of about $344B.

ni10.evidence: It reported a loss of $0.11 per share in 2016, within the last ten years, although it has been profitable every year since.

gr4.evidence: Caterpillar has paid dividends for decades and has raised them for 33 consecutive years, including an 8% increase in June 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a $0.11 loss in 2016 to $18.81 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The P/E of about 33 is far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 33 times P/B of about 18 is roughly 600, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its machines and engines are better than rivals' in reliability and support, but not ten times better.

timing.evidence: AI data-center power demand drove a 72% rise in Q2 2026 power-generation sales to users and a record $72B backlog.

th3.evidence: It has long been a large player in a large, established market.

team.evidence: The management team is experienced and executing well, but it is not a founder-led or legendary team.

th5.evidence: Its exclusive dealer network and Cat Financial give it unmatched reach to customers.

durable.evidence: Its brand, dealer network and installed base have kept it #1 for decades and should hold for 10-20 years, though electrification and Chinese rivals are risks.

th7.evidence: Its opportunities in data-center power and autonomy are also pursued by Cummins, Rolls-Royce, GE Vernova and Komatsu.

trend.evidence: It is a major beneficiary of AI data-center power demand, but most of its sales still come from cyclical construction and mining.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 adjusted EPS rose 73% to $8.17, and the consensus for 2026 EPS rose from $24.20 to $26.71 in August 2026.

dr2.evidence: A $72B backlog and new capacity support growth, but the market already expects strong 2026-2027 results.

dr4.evidence: High interest rates and diesel prices hurt construction demand, while infrastructure and energy spending help.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 earnings, data-center order announcements, IEEPA tariff recoveries and new engine capacity from Q4 2026 are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Earnings momentum is strong, but cyclicality and valuation make a large concentrated position hard to justify.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 33.8% in 2025 (38.0% in 2024), high for machinery but modest compared with software or brand businesses.

fcfyield.evidence: P/FCF is about 38, a free-cash-flow yield of about 2.6%, low for a cyclical business growing 5-7% a year over the long term.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 27, so operating profit is only about 3.6% of enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback: sales rose 24% in Q2 2026 and the backlog is at a record; only the share price has pulled back.

pa4.evidence: Its scale, brand and machinery balance sheet make permanent business impairment unlikely, though overpaying could cause lasting losses.

wo1.evidence: It leads in autonomous mining haulage (robotics) and supplies data-center power, but it is not an innovation-platform leader in ARK's sense.

wo2.evidence: Its product costs are not falling quickly with volume, and tariffs are adding about $2.2B of costs in 2026.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms in a meaningful way.

wo4.evidence: The company targets 5-7% annual sales growth through 2030, far from a many-fold expansion.

ac3.evidence: Demand depends on commodity prices (mining, oil and gas), interest rates and construction cycles.

ns1.evidence: It prices for margin rather than passing scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Services growth and data-center power should strengthen it, but competition from Chinese makers and electrification could offset this.

va2.evidence: It solves big, costly problems: moving earth and ore cheaply and reliably, and providing power where the grid cannot.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the AI/energy infrastructure trend through gensets and turbines, but it is an old machinery company benefiting from the trend, not one built for it.

tn2.evidence: The market long saw a cyclical machinery firm while power for data centers is a growing part of the business, but that shift is now widely recognised.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap U.S. industrial, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline or startup, though it is cyclical.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($8.9B in 2025) and revenue grew in 2025 and 2026; more debt than cash is mostly Cat Financial's customer lending, a valid reason.

tn5.evidence: MP&E free cash flow has been positive, but cash ($6.7B at June 2026) has been below total debt ($45.1B) in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: 2026 sales are guided up mid-to-high teens (Q2 +24%), but 2025 growth was 4.3% and the long-run target is 5-7%.

tn7.evidence: TTM revenue growth of roughly 18% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 12% is about 30, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2026 revenue is outgrowing costs: Q2 adjusted operating margin rose 430 basis points to 21.9%.

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: more debt ($45.1B) than cash ($6.7B), and a 2025 operating margin of 16.5% (TTM about 18.7%), below 20%.

tn10.evidence: It faces no major legal threat, but trade policy (about $2.2B of 2026 tariff costs) and emissions regulation are material.

tn11.evidence: It provides heavy machines, engines and power systems that help builders, miners and data-center owners move earth and make power reliably, and it charges through equipment sales, parts, services and financing; customers choose it for reliability and dealer support.

tn13.evidence: Total 85: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (1.8%), institutions 10 (73%), revenue vs expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 10, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2024, operating margin fell in 2025 and cash was below debt in every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is fine (2025 operating profit was about 6x total interest expense) and the current ratio is 1.37, but liabilities are 4.3x equity and non-goodwill assets are only about 1.2x liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Joe Creed has executed well but has been CEO only since May 2025, is not a founder and has no known open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: It beat consensus EPS in each of the last four quarters (Q3 2025 $4.95 vs $4.52 to Q2 2026 $8.17 vs $6.17).

tn21.evidence: There is no fraud, auditor change or acquisition spree, but operating margin declined in 2025 (20.2% to 16.5%) and insiders sell rather than buy.

tn22.evidence: It has $67.6B of revenue, strong profits and shrinking share count, with no hype-driven share sales.

tn24.evidence: The price (about 33 times trailing earnings) implies long-run growth well above the 5-7% the company itself targets, even though 2026 growth is high.

tn25.evidence: With about 4.6% average 3-year revenue growth and a roughly 12% FCF margin, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth give roughly $150 a share, far below the price of about $749.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 27 is high for a cyclical machinery maker, and the PEG is about 1.45, above 1.
